title: Ageing- and dementia-friendly design: theory and evidence from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology and environmental psychology can contribute to design guidelines that minimise spatial disorientation

findings.antecedent: Typical ageing
findings.consequent: Decline in spatial orientation and navigational skills, difficulty learning to navigate in new, unfamiliar environments
findings.quote: Spatial orientation and navigational skills start deteriorating relatively early in the ageing process, even when there are no apparent deficiencies in other cognitive abilities (Harris and Wolbers 2012; Moffat 2009).

findings.antecedent: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) or Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.consequent: Disorientation, especially in unfamiliar environments
findings.quote: This gradual loss of navigational skills is even more evident in individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) (Fasano et al. 2018; Mitolo et al. 2013) or AD, of which disorientation is typically one of the first symptoms (Pai and Jacobs 2004; Serino et al. 2015), and in unfamiliar environments.

findings.antecedent: Retirement complexes and care homes designed to reduce wayfinding difficulties
findings.consequent: Easier transition to new accommodation, improved independence, quality of life, well-being, and reduced caregiver workload for people with AD
findings.quote: Designing retirement complexes and care homes with people whose navigational skills are declining in mind would make the transition to their new environment easier for people with AD (O'Malley et al. 2017).

findings.antecedent: Spatial anxiety
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance in complex navigation tasks
findings.quote: For instance, spatial anxiety has a detrimental effect on wayfinding performance, particularly in complex navigation tasks (Srinivas 2011).

findings.antecedent: Sense of spatial self-efficacy and pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance
findings.quote: whereas a sense of spatial self-efficacy and taking pleasure in exploring unfamiliar environments positively correlate with wayfinding performance (Pazzaglia et al. 2018a, b).

findings.antecedent: Small-scale environments
findings.consequent: Reduction in dysfunctional behaviour, improved well-being (lessened depressive symptoms, improved mood, quality of life)
findings.quote: small-scale environments, an environmental aspect strictly related to spatial navigation (Marquardt and Schmieg 2009), are associated with the reduction in dysfunctional behaviour and improved well-being including lessened depressive symptoms and improved mood and quality of life.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks with properties: uniqueness, saliency, persistence, informativeness, nameability, relevant location
findings.consequent: Usefulness for orientation and wayfinding
findings.quote: To be useful for the purposes of orientation and wayfinding, landmarks must have a number of properties (Nothegger et al. 2004; Raubal and Winter 2002; Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a).

findings.antecedent: Cognitive ageing
findings.consequent: Decline in route learning ability (longer to learn novel routes, deficits in landmark-direction associations, impaired knowledge of landmark sequence)
findings.quote: Cognitive ageing is associated with a decline in route learning ability (Head and Isom 2010; Hilton et al. 2021) i.e., older adults take longer to learn novel routes (O'Malley et al. 2018).

findings.antecedent: Healthy older adults
findings.consequent: Deficits in using allocentric navigation strategies (longer to form cognitive maps, less efficient in planning new routes)
findings.quote: Healthy older adults also show deficits in using allocentric navigation strategies. Specifically, healthy older adults take longer to form cognitive maps and, in addition to their difficulty with encoding spatial information, their memory retrieval is also affected by cognitive ageing (Iaria et al. 2009).

findings.antecedent: Healthy older adults
findings.consequent: Preference for egocentric navigation strategies over allocentric, difficulty switching from egocentric to allocentric strategies
findings.quote: Specifically, older adults find allocentric navigation strategies more difficult to use than egocentric strategies (Wiener et al. 2013; Head and Isom 2010; Iaria et al. 2009) and, given the opportunity to choose, they prefer to use the latter (Rodgers et al. 2012).

findings.antecedent: Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.consequent: Spatial disorientation (early sign), severe navigation deficits (path integration, route learning, cognitive mapping)
findings.quote: Spatial disorientation is one of the earliest signs of AD (Pai and Jacobs 2004), and recent research even suggests that adults at a higher genetic risk of AD show signs of navigation deficits decades before they may develop AD (Kunz et al. 2015; Coughlan et al. 2019).

findings.antecedent: Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.consequent: More pronounced impairments in hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory tasks than egocentric parietal memory tasks
findings.quote: While AD affects both egocentric and allocentric navigation tasks, these effects seem more pronounced in spatial tasks that require a hippocampal-dependent allocentric memory, such as locating object or landmarks relative to the environment, rather than in tasks which can be solved with egocentric parietal memory in which object locations are remembered relative to the navigator (Kalova et al. 2005; Burgess et al. 2006).

findings.antecedent: Good design for navigation (navigability)
findings.consequent: Key aspect of environmental quality
findings.quote: In environmental psychology, navigability is related to good design for navigation, a key aspect of environmental quality (Zimring 1982, 1990).

findings.antecedent: Certain environmental features (large buildings, complex layouts, too many route options/choice points/corners, limited visual access, uniformity)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding difficulties, waste of time/money, increased cognitive/physical effort, impatience/hostility
findings.quote: Certain environmental features can generate wayfinding difficulties, particularly in large buildings or environments, that cause a waste of time and money (Zimring 1990), add to users' cognitive and physical effort (Carlson et al. 2010), and make users impatient with, or even hostile towards public buildings that are difficult to navigate (Berkeley 1973; Dixon 1968; McKean 1972).

findings.antecedent: Varying sizes, shapes, architectural styles, colours within a building (visual differentiation); low levels of spatial differentiation (repetition of similar elements, symmetrical structures)
findings.consequent: Positive effects on navigability (visual differentiation); problems with orientation (spatial uniformity)
findings.quote: Varying sizes, shapes, architectural styles and colours within a building can have positive effects on its navigability (Gärling et al. 1986).

findings.antecedent: Small-scale units with good visual access
findings.consequent: Reduced spatial disorientation, makes spatial memory/recall and wayfinding decisions redundant
findings.quote: The most effective layouts for care homes are small-scale units where everything a resident needs is always in view (visual access) from wherever they are within the facility (Caspi 2014).

findings.antecedent: Places (bedrooms, communal spaces) that are easily recognisable and meaningful (e.g., portraits, name signs, memory boxes, different furniture/color schemes/wallpaper, functional names)
findings.consequent: Improved recognition, easier navigation/orientation, support for decision points
findings.quote: The efficiency of their spatial navigation depends on people's ability to immediately recognise the place they are in or navigating to.

findings.antecedent: Corridors with clearly different design features (themes, colours, frames, entrances), visible from decision points
findings.consequent: Reduced disorientation, aid simple landmark-based navigation, compensate for impaired path integration
findings.quote: In large built environments, corridors often look very similar, and this is the most frequently mentioned factor causing disorientation in people with memory problems or dementia.

findings.antecedent: Brightly coloured, high-contrast objects used as landmarks
findings.consequent: Easier to remember and recognise for older adults/dementia patients, aid navigation
findings.quote: Objects that serve as landmarks need to be remembered and recognised. Older adults and people with dementia remember and recognise brightly coloured, high-contrast objects more easily than less-striking objects in pastel shades (Cernin et al. 2003).

findings.antecedent: Concrete, easy-to-name landmarks/cues
findings.consequent: Support verbal encoding of landmarks, counter word-finding problems in dementia
findings.quote: To counter the increasing word-finding problems associated with dementia (Rohrer et al. 2008) and to support the verbal encoding of landmarks, it is crucial to choose landmarks or cues that are concrete, rather than abstract (such as an abstract painting), and therefore easy to name.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks unique in both visual appearance and verbal encoding
findings.consequent: Unambiguous identification of places, reduced confusion/disorientation
findings.quote: As discussed above, landmarks need to be unique in order to identify a place unambiguously (Stankiewicz and Kalia 2007a). Since they can be encoded both visually and verbally, it is important to ensure that they are distinguishable in both domains.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks located at decision points (junctions, open areas) or visible from them (beacons)
findings.consequent: Better remembered, aid navigation (associative cues, beacons), less memory demanding (beacons)
findings.quote: Generally, people navigating along a route remember landmarks that are located at decision points better than those located elsewhere along the route (Aginsky et al. 1997).

findings.antecedent: Signage and maps
findings.consequent: Overcome orientation/navigation problems, externalise spatial knowledge, compensate for declining cognitive abilities
findings.quote: Signage and maps can be used to overcome many orientation and navigation problems. Signage and maps essentially externalise spatial knowledge, decision-making and spatial planning, and can therefore compensate for declining cognitive abilities (Passini et al. 2000).

findings.antecedent: Signage with both icons and text, familiar icons, simple/uncluttered, clear contrast, placed at eye level or lower
findings.consequent: Improved recognition/understanding, aid navigation, reduced falls risk
findings.quote: Signage should therefore not rely on textual information alone, but also contain pictures or icons.

findings.antecedent: More personal environmental cues/features (pictures, memorable spaces) vs. institutional signage/YAH maps
findings.consequent: Preferred by care home residents (homely feel), but challenge to integrate effective signage without detracting from homely feel
findings.quote: most of the care home residents interviewed in a recent study said they preferred more personal environmental cues or features, such as relevant pictures and memorable spaces, over signage or maps (O'Malley et al. 2017).

findings.antecedent: You-are-here (YAH) maps oriented so 'up' on map aligns with straight ahead in real environment
findings.consequent: Minimised cognitive effort, reduced need for mental rotation
findings.quote: It is important for YAH maps to be oriented so that 'up' on the map is aligned with straight ahead in the real environment (McKenzie and Klippel 2016).

findings.antecedent: You-are-here (YAH) maps
findings.consequent: Little use as navigation aids for people with dementia (often discarded, prefer landmarks)
findings.quote: There is currently only a handful of neuropsychological studies on map usage by older adults and people with dementia, but the available evidence suggests that maps in general, and even YAH maps, are of little use to them.

findings.antecedent: Alzheimer's disease (AD)
findings.consequent: Affects ability to discriminate between colours (blue/green range), less sensitive to contrast (needs stronger contrast)
findings.quote: It should be noted at this point that AD affects people's ability to discriminate between colours, particularly in the blue and green range, and less so in the red and yellow range (Wijk and Sivik 1995).

findings.antecedent: Semantic dementia
findings.consequent: Colour naming becomes problematic
findings.quote: Colour naming and being able to make correct choices about colour becomes particularly problematic in patients with semantic dementia, which appears to be caused by the breakdown of conceptual knowledge (Rogers et al. 2007).

findings.antecedent: Brightness or darkness of a colour (lighter-coloured walls, less-contrasting furnishings)
findings.consequent: Affects space perception (sense of spaciousness or confinement)
findings.quote: Space perception (i.e. a sense of spaciousness or confinement) is affected by the brightness or darkness of a colour, rather than by a specific colour or shade. A sense of spaciousness can be enhanced by lighter-coloured walls and less-contrasting furnishings (Tofle et al. 2004).

findings.antecedent: Sufficient light levels and suitable colours (extra light, bright strong colours)
findings.consequent: Important for creating supportive environments, help residents find their way, improve object recall
findings.quote: The use of extra light and contrasting colours can help care home residents find their way more easily (Noell-Waggoner 2002; Netten 1989).

findings.antecedent: Personalising bedroom colours (given stable colour preferences in AD)
findings.consequent: Effective way to help care home residents recognise their own room
findings.quote: The fact that colour preferences seem to remain stable in people with AD (Wijk and Sivik 1995) suggests that personalising bedroom colours could be an effective way to help care home residents recognise their own room.
